title: Engineering habits
why: The gap between someone who can code and an engineer is mostly habits: version control, tests, structure and code that others can review. These are what a take-home reviewer looks at first.
outcomes: Work in branches and pull requests, even solo
Write tests with pytest, including edge cases
Keep code clean with Ruff and a type checker
Lay out a project so a stranger can install, run and test it
lessons: Git beyond basics: branches, pull requests, merge conflicts, clear commit messages
Testing with pytest: fixtures and parametrise, edge cases first
Lint and format with Ruff; type-check with pyright or mypy
Project layout: src layout, pyproject.toml, uv lockfile
Write a README with install, run, test and design notes
Command line fluency: navigation, grep, pipes, environment variables
method: Work in small loops: write a failing test, make it pass, commit. Open a pull request against your own repo for every feature so review and CI become reflex.
build: Turn the Python module's tool into a package with tests (80% coverage or more), clean Ruff output and a visible pull-request history.

o: A whole day's work in one go
One logical change with a clear message
As large as possible to save time
quiz.e: Small, single-purpose commits are easy to review, revert and understand later.

quiz.q: By default, pytest discovers tests in:
o: Files named test_*.py, functions named test_*
quiz.e: pytest collects test_*.py (or *_test.py) files and test_ functions.

quiz.q: Are Python type hints enforced at runtime?
o: No, tools like pyright or mypy check them
quiz.e: Hints are for checkers and readers. Pydantic is one library that does validate at runtime.

quiz.q: Why use a branch and pull request when working alone?
o: It isolates changes, shows a reviewable diff and runs CI before merge
quiz.e: The PR is your own review gate and a visible record of how you work.
Secrets and generated folders stay out of Git; source, config and tests go in.
